Share
GULF OF OMAN — The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) center issued Warning 120-26 after the master of an oil tanker reported the ship struck by an unknown projectile 9 nautical miles (10 miles, 17 kilometers) northeast of Ash Shishah, Oman.
UKMTO logged the report at 8:25 p.m. UTC on August 24 and classified the event as an attack. The master said the projectile damaged the engine room and left the tanker unable to proceed. UKMTO said the crew was reported safe and that environmental impact was unknown in the initial warning.
The stated position sits on the eastern face of Oman’s Musandam Peninsula, on the Gulf of Oman approach to the Strait of Hormuz.
The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC), in an advisory issued August 23 with information current to 3:00 p.m. UTC that day, rated the strait SEVERE and recorded no confirmed attacks in the prior 48 hours.
Warning 120-26 is the first UKMTO attack product on that corridor after that cutoff.
In a separate incident the same calendar day, UKMTO Warning 119-26 said a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile 63 nautical miles (72 miles, 117 kilometers) west of Yanbu, Saudi Arabia, with a fire on the main deck.
That event is in the Red Sea, not the Gulf of Oman.

Bottom line: Actuators — motor, reducer and screw — consume more than 50% of a humanoid robot's hardware cost, and core components together exceed 60%.
Over the past three years, this largest cost block traced a steep decline: frameless torque motors fell from RMB 2,000 to around RMB 500, and same-spec reducers from RMB 1,280 to RMB 410. But falling prices are not free — the selection logic has to change with them.
What exactly makes a humanoid robot expensive?
* Cost item | Share / amount | Note
* Actuators (motor + reducer + screw) | Over 50% of total hardware cost | The robot's joints
* Dexterous hands | 20–25% of hardware cost | Each hand needs several micro motors
* Core components combined | Over 60% | Including sensors and encoders
* Frameless torque motor | One per actuator across 28 units; ~RMB 1,200 each → about RMB 33,600 per robot , or 10.63% of BOM | Main rotary joint solution

Sources: public industry estimates, Tonghuashun, 2026-09.
One comparison is easy to miss: a six-axis industrial robot uses only six servo axes, while Tesla's Optimus has 28 body joints and more than 50 degrees of freedom including the hands. That order-of-magnitude difference in joint count is the root cause of the dramatic shift in servo volume and cost structure.

It prioritizes the signals that reflect mechanical stress, actuation health, thermal load, motion quality, and control-system anomalies in ways that remain meaningful across repeated robot operation.
System-level issues include positioning accuracy, load capacity, and overall stability. Component-level issues include electric actuators, motors, speed reducers, sensors, belts, bolts, and other joint-related elements. Predictive maintenance works only when the monitored signals line up with those real failure modes.
FANUC’s ZDT materials are a useful example of what practical robot monitoring looks like in the field: they highlight reducer deterioration on each axis, battery charge and memory status, alarm and operation history, consumable lifetimes, and process-related abnormalities such as servo-gun issues.
These signals are attractive because they are close to the actuation chain, often already available through the controller or drive, and sensitive to changes in mechanical resistance, brake problems, reducer deterioration, and abnormal loading.
The recent review literature on industrial robot diagnostics makes this point clearly.
Vibration is one of the most powerful predictive-maintenance signals in industry, and robots are no exception. It is especially useful for gear and reducer degradation, looseness, fastening problems, and some mechanical faults that may not show up clearly in controller-level averages.

The Department of Defense (DOD) broke ground on the Project Pele transportable microreactor project at Idaho National Laboratory (INL).
The demonstration project is being led by DOD’s Strategic Capabilities Office and could be one of the first advanced reactors to operate in the United States as early as 2026.
Project Pele Breaks Ground
DOD is planning to design, build, and demonstrate a transportable high-temperature gas reactor that will operate at the lab’s Critical Infrastructure Test Range Complex.
The reactor will be manufactured by BWX Technologies and connected to INL’s microgrid producing 1 to 5 megawatts of electrical power.
Project Pele is a whole-of-government effort, with critical expertise provided by the Department of Energy, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, NASA, and the National Nuclear Security Administration.
The reactor is expected to operate for a minimum of three years at the lab and will help demonstrate the use of clean, reliable, and transportable nuclear power to help meet the increasing energy demands at military bases across the country.

By Eve Sampson
Wednesday, Aug 26, 2026
An artistic rendering depicts GA-TES at a notional military installation. (General Atomics)
The Army is investing billions of dollars to bring nuclear power to military bases, selecting five companies to build nuclear microreactors at installations across the U.S., the service announced Wednesday in collaboration with the Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit.
The service said it expects to field more than 20 microreactors across Department of Defense installations.
The agreements, worth up to $2.2 billion combined, mark a step in the Army’s Janus program, an initiative that aims to introduce microreactors to power installations independently rather than relying on civilian electrical grids.
The Army introduced the program in 2025 after an executive order called for the military to speed up its integration of nuclear power, with the goal of having an operational reactor at a military base by Sept. 30, 2028.
“Awarding these contracts accelerates our ability to deliver safe, reliable baseload power directly to our installations,” Secretary of the Army Dan Driscoll said in a release. “We are building the energy resilience necessary to project combat power globally, without relying on potentially vulnerable external grids.”
